stories.headline: Trump waives Russia sanctions; bipartisan backlash grows

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

facts: President Trump signed an executive order Friday night suspending sanctions on Russia that were set to take effect Sunday.
The sanctions stem from the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a law Trump signed last month after the Senate passed it 86-11.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the suspension amounts to a 60-day pause to let the administration assess the economic impact of the sanctions.

The law authorized tariffs of up to 100% on countries importing large amounts of Russian oil and gas, including top buyers China and India, and targeted senior Russian officials, financial institutions and Russia's 'shadow fleet' of tankers.
Congress is on recess until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, limiting any immediate legislative response to Trump's order.
Rep. Gregory Meeks introduced legislation Friday aimed at blocking a separate Trump-brokered deal to import Russian diesel.
Sen. Lindsey Graham, who championed the sanctions bill, died earlier this year.
Ukrainian officials reported at least nine people killed and about 60 injured in Russian strikes since Friday, including an ambulance driver killed in Kherson.
ladder.analysis: The dispute centers on a sweeping Russia sanctions law that passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and was designed to choke off funding for Moscow's war in Ukraine by targeting its oil exports, financial institutions and shipping networks. Trump's decision to suspend enforcement just before the law's effective date marks a sharp reversal from the legislative intent, and it comes alongside other recent moves — a U.S. deal to import Russian diesel and reported disruptions to Ukraine's Starlink access — that have fueled concerns in Washington and Kyiv about the administration's posture toward Moscow. With lawmakers in recess until after the midterms, Congress has no immediate mechanism to challenge the executive order, leaving the suspension's 60-day review period as the near-term determinant of what, if any, sanctions take effect.

ladder.steelman: Despite sharp partisan rhetoric, lawmakers across both parties who spoke out agree on the substance: the sanctions law passed with near-unanimous support and should be enforced, suggesting the disagreement is less about policy toward Russia than about whether the executive branch can unilaterally override a bipartisan congressional mandate.
ladder.implications: With Congress in recess until after the midterms, the 60-day review period cited by Secretary Rubio will likely determine whether any of the suspended sanctions are eventually reinstated, and lawmakers' ability to formally challenge the waiver — or related moves like the Russian diesel deal — will depend on legislative action once they return to Washington.

stories.headline: Ukraine launches massive drone attack on Russia, hitting St Petersburg oil terminal
body: Ukraine launched one of its largest drone attacks of the war on Russia overnight Saturday, striking the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal and other targets in and around Russia's second-largest city. The attack killed at least one person and wounded five others, according to St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov. Fires broke out at the oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district, while a logistics center belonging to e-commerce company Ozon and a data center operated by social network VK were also hit. Russia's Defense Ministry said it shot down 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 regions, and local officials reported that about 20,000 people were left without electricity after transformer substations were struck. Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed, and 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the city.

The strikes came as Kyiv defied U.S. President Donald Trump's demand that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Trump had announced an "energy ceasefire" a week earlier, saying both sides had agreed to stop striking each other's energy facilities. Ukraine paused its strikes for three days after the announcement but accused Russia of continuing its attacks and then resumed operations earlier this week. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday that since Trump declared the ceasefire, Russia had deliberately attacked Ukraine's energy and oil and gas sectors 76 times. "Last night alone, there were strikes on substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions," he wrote on X, adding that tens of thousands of families remained without power. Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight killed at least two people and injured a dozen others, according to Zelensky. Over the past week, he said, Russia had attacked Ukraine with nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, with energy facilities the main target.

The attack on St. Petersburg underlined the deteriorating relationship between Kyiv and Washington. Trump has called Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil facilities a "disgrace" and repeatedly pressed Zelensky to stop them. On Friday, the Trump administration waived a sweeping new sanctions package passed by Congress that would have expanded measures targeting Russia's oil and gas industry, and suspended sanctions on imports of Russian diesel as part of a deal Trump struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Zelensky criticized the move, saying it amounted to the U.S. investing in Russia's war effort and encouraging Putin to keep fighting. The White House said the waiver was a 60-day pause to analyze the impact of sanctions on the global economy. The decisions drew criticism even from some U.S. Republicans.

Zelensky also said that Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite internet system, crucial for guiding its drones, had been restricted. He said that at speeds above 161 kilometers per hour, Starlink shuts down and Ukraine loses the drone, and that the restrictions also prevented Ukraine from using the system to shoot down Russian drones. "The restrictions are in effect on Ukrainian territory, but they do not apply within the European Union," he said. "In other words, this is a planned operation … to restrict us, cut us off and prevent us from defending ourselves." The Trump administration denied restricting the service. Kyiv also said it was now facing Russian ballistic missile attacks without alerts from allies, raising concerns that the U.S. might further limit intelligence sharing.

Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified strikes on each other's energy infrastructure as the war enters its fifth year. Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, but the United Nations noted that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years. Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising fears of another freezing winter. Zelensky said energy workers and repair crews were working around the clock to restore electricity. The attack on St. Petersburg, which Russian state media called the largest on the region in four years, demonstrated Ukraine's willingness to keep striking deep inside Russia despite U.S. pressure, as Kyiv argues that targeting Russian oil facilities limits the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort.

stories.headline: French police arrest about 1,800 as protests turn violent across country
body: French police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets in nationwide protests that were largely peaceful but turned violent in parts of the country, leaving burnt-out cars, shattered shopfronts and looted stores across Paris and other cities. Protesters, including students, trade unionists and Yellow Vest activists, were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the high cost of living, social inequality and deteriorating public services such as schools. France's interior ministry said more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured in the unrest.

Violence unfolded in Paris and cities including Marseille, Lille, Lyon, Limoges and Saint-Étienne. In the capital, riot police fired tear gas and water cannon at protesters, charged crowds and were seen striking people with batons; groups set fires in streets, torched vehicles and gutted at least one restaurant, and the BBC witnessed fighting among some groups. Designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace had their glass frontages smashed, and the Retail and Trade Federation said about 1,500 shops and retailers were damaged. Looting was reported in Paris, Marseille, Lille, Nice and Bordeaux, according to AFP. In Lille, a McDonald's was set on fire and an Apple store was looted; in Marseille, protesters used a metal fence as a battering ram to enter the city hall; and in Lille, protesters also broke into and vandalized the city hall. Clashes were reported near the Gare du Nord train station and in the Saint-Denis area on the outskirts of Paris.

The interior ministry said the arrests followed "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in cities including Paris, Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers, involving "attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets." The windows of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in western Paris were broken, and damage was reported in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence. In Lyon, the city's tourist office was set alight; Mayor Grégory Doucet called it "a tragedy" for a "very iconic, well-known historic building," and police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from tackling the blaze. In Limoges, the 143-year-old town hall was "largely lost" after being deliberately set on fire, with parts of the building collapsing; Prefect Maurice Barate blamed a "wild horde." In Saint-Étienne, Mayor Régis Juanico said a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive, adding, "Such a tragedy should never have happened."

Paris residents described the aftermath as akin to war. "It's like we had a war," Mehmet Ozeden told AFP. Resident Anita GrasIt said it was "terrifying" to see young people "smashing everything, with total impunity," while another resident, Maryse, said looters were "proudly carrying supermarket baskets filled with goods and laughing about their thefts." A shop owner near the Place de la République whose ransacked store he watched on CCTV told the BBC that looters spent over an hour and a half inside without police appearing, and said he did not believe they were genuine protesters. CCTV footage aired by France's Channel 2 showed masked teenagers helping themselves to items in a mobile phone shop. On Sunday, shopkeepers swept up glass and rubbish trucks cleared debris as graffiti reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich" was daubed on stores; the BBC also reported the Good Vibes bakery's glass front was shattered and the Nicolas wine store had every bottle either stolen or smashed, leaving a lingering smell of alcohol.

The protests began late last month as student demonstrations over school conditions, including teacher absences, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings, with demands for greater investment. They widened as trade unionists and remnants of the Yellow Vests ("Gilets jaunes") movement joined; that movement staged weekly protests from November 2018 to June 2020, initially against fuel price rises and later against the cost of living and economic inequality. Hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has backed the student protests and marched in a demonstration on Tuesday, and the government has accused LFI of "pouring fuel on the fire of widespread public discontent," a charge the party denied. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu visited officers in Paris on Saturday evening, saying "It's a miracle the toll wasn't higher"; he put the arrests at about 1,200 and said 150 police officers had been injured.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, "several thousand far-left individuals" committed "outrages" determined to target public buildings and confront police, later joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses." He also said 110,000 people took part in demonstrations in Paris alone and that 110 marches had occurred nationwide. President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence on X, writing: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished." Police had banned rallies around the Élysée presidential palace, the prime minister's office and the Champs-Élysées, as well as a march through central Paris. DW correspondent Jack Parrock reported that most people on the streets "were teachers, nurses, students, and workers, who want no part in the unrest" but expressed "a collective rage against a government they don't feel is listening to them," while police appeared to "show some restraint" and try to de-escalate tensions.

stories.headline: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank; EU, US condemn surge in violence
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters, AP
body: A delegation of European diplomats was attacked by masked Israeli settlers on Saturday in the occupied West Bank, drawing condemnation from Belgium, France, the European Union and the United States. The diplomats — from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church — had traveled to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah to assess the situation on the ground after near-daily settler attacks on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest. Video footage showed masked settlers confronting the convoy; reports indicate stones were thrown. A car from the Belgian consulate had a window smashed, and a French mayor, Bernard Baudoux, was assaulted. Baudoux told AFP he was kicked, beaten with iron bars and thrown to the ground. “It’s the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me,” he said. “The whole world needs to know what’s happening there.”

Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice and ensure the safety of diplomats, journalists and Palestinians. He added that Belgium would continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for the violence. France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, called on Israeli authorities to “urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations.” Poland’s foreign affairs ministry also called for a “firm response” from Israeli authorities and an end to “the spiral of violence in the West Bank.” The EU condemned the attacks, urged Israel to abide by international and human rights law, and called for an end to the expansion of settlements. A spokesperson said the bloc expects “full accountability as well as effective measures” to stop the continued violence against Palestinians and journalists.

The attack came a day after Israeli settlers injured several Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, in a separate assault in another West Bank village. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the attack on Levine “disturbing” and “not a good look,” and urged Israel to “crack down” on the violence. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, described the assault as a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards” and said the assailants must face “prosecution to the fullest extent of the law.”

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) condemned what they called “the severe act of violence” and said they were investigating. According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar condemned the violence by what he called “Israeli rioters” but noted that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance, which could have helped safeguard the visitors. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office urged “caution before drawing conclusions,” suggesting the reports could be part of a “coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest.” The office said Israeli police and forensic investigators had launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible.

Critics argue that mere condemnations without consequences will not deter settler violence, which they say flourishes within a system of occupation, settlement expansion and impunity. Ahmed Najar, a Palestinian political analyst, told Al Jazeera: “Western governments continue to arm, fund and diplomatically protect Israel while treating settler attacks as isolated acts by a few extremists. But this violence flourishes within a wider system of occupation, settlement expansion and impunity.” Sven Kuhn von Burgsdorff, former EU representative to the occupied West Bank and Gaza, said the “lame protests” issued by European chancelleries are “pathetic” because they are not followed by concrete punitive measures. He noted that at the last Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Brussels on October 12, EU ministers were still unable to decide on sanctioning violent settlers or their enablers.

Israeli settler attacks during this year’s olive harvest season have already surpassed 2025 totals, according to Al Jazeera. On Saturday alone, settlers injured six Palestinians as Israeli forces arrested farmers during attacks across the West Bank. Four women and a child were among the injured in Ma’in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society. In Deir Ammar town, west of Ramallah, Israeli forces opened fire on farmers picking olives, forcing them to leave their land. The violence has prompted calls from the EU, the US and European governments for Israel to ensure the safety of civilians, journalists and diplomats, and to hold perpetrators accountable.

The IDF said they were investigating.
According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar condemned the violence by what he called 'Israeli rioters.'
Sa’ar noted that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance, which could have helped safeguard the visitors.

Netanyahu’s office suggested the reports could be part of a 'coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest.'
Netanyahu’s office said Israeli police and forensic investigators had launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible.

Ahmed Najar, a Palestinian political analyst, told Al Jazeera: 'Western governments continue to arm, fund and diplomatically protect Israel while treating settler attacks as isolated acts by a few extremists.'
Ahmed Najar said: 'But this violence flourishes within a wider system of occupation, settlement expansion and impunity.'

Sven Kuhn von Burgsdorff, former EU representative to the occupied West Bank and Gaza, said the 'lame protests' issued by European chancelleries are 'pathetic' because they are not followed by concrete punitive measures.
Kuhn von Burgsdorff noted that at the last Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Brussels on October 12, EU ministers were still unable to decide on sanctioning violent settlers or their enablers.
Israeli settler attacks during this year’s olive harvest season have already surpassed 2025 totals, according to Al Jazeera.
On Saturday alone, settlers injured six Palestinians as Israeli forces arrested farmers during attacks across the West Bank.
Four women and a child were among the injured in Ma’in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.
In Deir Ammar town, west of Ramallah, Israeli forces opened fire on farmers picking olives, forcing them to leave their land.
The violence has prompted calls from the EU, the US and European governments for Israel to ensure the safety of civilians, journalists and diplomats, and to hold perpetrators accountable.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy says Starlink restrictions still hamper Ukraine's drone defenses; Rubio confirms Starshield request under discussion
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite service. Speaking in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit, Zelenskyy said: "Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds. They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately."

Zelenskyy said Kyiv was in dialogue with U.S. officials and had been told the restrictions were linked to technical issues, but that "nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now." He described the effect in detail: "Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off. In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity." Ukrainian officials had said last week that restrictions on Starlink terminals slowed some drones on the battlefield.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, confirmed that Starshield is "not at this moment available to Ukraine," and said Kyiv's request for access to the system to conduct deep strikes inside Russia is "under discussion." He stressed the distinction between the two services: "Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it's regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defence product, a military product." Rubio rejected Zelenskyy's suggestion that the disruption was deliberate, saying, "No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn't use it," and adding that the service had reportedly been restored to its previous level. He also said, "I don't know what Zelenskyy said, I'm not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate."

Starlink has been central to Ukraine's communications, reconnaissance and drone operations since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. According to the Center for Security Studies at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025, enabling troops to communicate when infrastructure is destroyed, relay orders, and receive drone footage. The system became vital after the KA-SAT satellite system Ukraine previously favored was targeted in a cyberattack hours before the invasion. While Starlink and Starshield are based on the same technological infrastructure, Starshield is designed specifically for governmental and military use, offering deeper encryption, and SpaceX says it is primarily used by U.S. defense agencies and other government partners.

The speed restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at up to 300 km/h; if the connection is lost, live video can no longer be transmitted and drones effectively fly blind. Rubio said the United States had not ordered Starlink speeds to be reduced and that the service was back to what it was before. Separately, Zelenskyy criticized the Trump administration's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas. Europe has alternatives to Starlink such as Eutelsat/OneWeb, but their performance in wartime conditions has not been tested on a large scale, and Ukraine also relies on U.S.-provided reconnaissance data, which U.S. limits on access would compound.

Rubio said the U.S. government was not responsible for the outage, alleging that Ukraine's military has never had access to Starshield and has only been using Starlink. "Starshield is a contract with the U.S. military, it has nothing to do with Ukraine," he said. "I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield, they do not have Starshield now." Musk has said Starshield systems are controlled by the U.S. government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

stories.headline: Big Tech earnings week ahead: Meta, Tesla, Netflix and others report as AI-boom costs weigh on markets
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on AP
body: The third-quarter earnings season accelerates this week, with 70 S&P 500 companies reporting, led by a cluster of Big Tech names including Meta Platforms, Tesla and Netflix. The reports come after both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite fell last week as traders rotated out of technology stocks over concerns about mounting debt from the artificial-intelligence build-out, while markets also contend with high inflation and continued geopolitical tensions. Meta, reporting Wednesday after the close, will release its first quarterly results since launching AI agent Muse on Sept. 8; its stock has shot up more than 15% since then, and analysts are broadly bullish, with LSEG data showing expected earnings per share growth of 460% from a year earlier. Tesla, also reporting Wednesday after the close, is expected to post a 14.5% drop in earnings per share and nearly a 1% decline in revenue, with Wolfe Research citing a "tough quarter for Auto stocks" and eyeing a potential SpaceX merger and the robotaxi business as possible positives; Tesla's third-quarter deliveries fell 2% from a year earlier but still topped estimates.

Netflix reports Tuesday after the close, with analysts expecting 40% earnings growth from the year-earlier period, according to LSEG. But the streaming giant's stock has fallen the trading day after each of its last five earnings reports, by an average of 6.9%, including a 7.3% drop after its July 2026 report; the streak runs from July 2025 through July 2026. Netflix also last week announced plans to lay off about 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, and replaced its chief content officer. Barclays analyst Kannan Venkateshwar wrote that while Originals make up more than 60% of Netflix's titles, many viewers still see it "as a service for library content," adding, "The issue may not be Netflix itself but rather that the world around Netflix has changed and Netflix hasn't really changed enough with it."

Other major reports include General Motors, also Tuesday before the bell, where analysts expect nearly a 30% jump in earnings per share but flat revenue; JPMorgan analysts maintained their overweight rating but lowered their price target, citing a likely cautious 2027 outlook and affordability concerns after vehicle sales declined 5.5% in the quarter. United Airlines and American Airlines both face high fuel costs; United is expected to show revenue growth above 15% but declining EPS, while American is expected to post top-line growth of 18% as it pushes premium seating — CEO Robert Isom said last month that 30% of seats generate half of the airline's revenue. AT&T reports Wednesday, with expected earnings growth of nearly 11% but slower revenue growth of 3.2%, after a SpaceX spectrum acquisition sparked a telecom sell-off. Procter & Gamble reports Thursday, with analysts expecting revenue growth just shy of 2% and a 5.4% decline in earnings; Citi maintained a buy rating, citing potential upside in the U.S. and China. Also reporting Wednesday after the close are IBM, Texas Instruments, Lam Research and SAP, while Intel reports Oct. 29. Monday has no major tech earnings.

The week's data calendar is light: weekly jobless claims arrive Thursday and S&P Global's flash PMIs for October come Friday. Federal Reserve officials will not steer sentiment, as the central bank's quiet period covers every trading day ahead of its Oct. 27-28 meeting. Semiconductors have been under pressure, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) down 11.8% over the previous week. The earnings season got off to a strong start last week: about 45 S&P 500 companies have reported, with 85% exceeding earnings estimates, according to FactSet, though the big banks were mixed — Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and Citigroup beat on earnings and revenue, Wells Fargo was mixed, and JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America missed on both lines.

Overall, the reporting period could shift investor attention toward corporate fundamentals after recent market volatility, according to JPMorgan strategists led by Mislav Matejka, who expect third-quarter earnings growth to broaden beyond artificial-intelligence-related companies across U.S. and European equities. Consensus estimates from IBES show S&P 500 earnings per share up 24% for the quarter, while FactSet and LSEG point to growth of 30%. Historical patterns suggest big post-earnings moves for several of this week's reporters: Meta beats estimates 88% of the time but fell 8% after its last topline miss; Tesla has missed in two of the last four quarters and posts a topline beat only 58% of the time, having averaged a 7.8% move in either direction after each of its last eight reports; Netflix has fallen after five straight reports; and both GM and American Airlines beat estimates 89% and 88% of the time, respectively.

stories.headline: Fed's Warsh Avoids Signal on Rate Move as Inflation Persists
body: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday he won't prejudge what the U.S. central bank will do about interest rates at its upcoming meetings in October and December, offering no fresh signals during a "fireside chat" with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok.

The Fed increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9% in September, its first increase in three years. Stubbornly elevated U.S. inflation will likely lead it to hike that rate again in coming months to slow spending and help cool price pressures. According to minutes released from the most recent meeting, most Fed officials expect another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year. Such a move would raise borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans, and credit cards over time.

"At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago," Warsh said. "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."

The September rate hike defied U.S. President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates. The president criticized the Fed's rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The global surge in prices is a key concern of central bankers and financial leaders meeting in Bangkok.

Warsh said the surge in investment driven by the craze for artificial intelligence is one of the factors behind higher inflation, and the Fed's task force on issues related to AI will meet Nov. 16. "I'd say the advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime to this point," he said. Unlike military conflict and other shocks that are driving prices higher, Warsh said he believes AI will bring "huge benefit" to the world economy in time.

For Fed economists who struggle to foresee the future using data that lags behind today's realities, AI could prove a vital tool, he said. "We torture data with old fashioned models to try to find out what's underlying inflation trends. Not so long from now, it won't be torture. We will have access at the fingertips of central banks to all the information in the world, and we'll be able to use new analytical tools to distill that data," he said.

stories.headline: Rays beat Guardians to tie ALCS
body: The Tampa Bay Rays evened the American League Championship Series at two games apiece on Saturday, defeating the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 at Progressive Field in a game delayed a day by heavy rain. The victory sets up a best-of-three finish for a spot in the World Series against the Milwaukee Brewers, with Game 5 scheduled for 5 p.m. ET Sunday. The rain postponement erased the series' second travel day, meaning Games 4 through 7 would be played on four consecutive days if necessary.

Tampa Bay's offense, which had scored as many as four runs only twice in eight postseason games entering Saturday, broke out against a Guardians bullpen anchored by Foster Griffin. The Rays tied the game in the top of the third when Yandy Díaz hit a two-out double and Jonathan Aranda drove Díaz in two pitches later. Junior Caminero, who had been quiet in the postseason, gave the Rays a 2-1 lead in the sixth inning with an RBI double. Tampa Bay added three insurance runs in the seventh, and Díaz sealed the margin with a two-run homer in the top of the ninth.

Caminero nearly homered in the fourth inning, launching a fly ball with an exit velocity of 110.7 mph and a 29-degree launch angle — a combination that had produced a home run on every one of 180 previous similar occasions at the ballpark. But the mid-40s temperature in Cleveland kept the ball in play, and Guardians center fielder Petey Halpin caught it at the wall. Caminero, who tied for the AL lead with 42 homers during the regular season, remained homer-less in the postseason but delivered the go-ahead double two innings later.

The Guardians rallied in the bottom of the seventh, stringing together four straight two-out hits to score two runs and cut the Rays' lead to 5-3. The inning ended when Steven Kwan grounded out to first base with the tying run on base, sliding in headfirst and busting his lip in the process; he remained in the game with a bandage. Rays manager Kevin Cash said after the game, "Overall, just happy that Junior squared some balls up, Aranda came through in a big way for us and then Yandy there at the end with a two-run, add-on homer."

The series now shifts to a best-of-three format. Game 5 will feature Drew Rasmussen starting for the Rays and Parker Messick for the Guardians. The winner of the ALCS will face the Milwaukee Brewers, who have not played since Thursday, in the Fall Classic.

stories.headline: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope Exceeds Expectations by Nearly 30%
body: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has achieved optical performance nearly 30% better than predicted after engineers completed a series of precision adjustments, including moving a mirror by about one-sixteenth the width of a human hair. The work, announced by NASA on October 17, 2026, brings the telescope’s powerful instruments into near-perfect alignment, promising exceptionally sharp cosmic surveys.

The telescope’s Wide Field Instrument, its main camera system, now produces image quality with an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square), substantially better than the pre-launch requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS. To put that scale into perspective, 90 nanometers is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a human hair. The improvement means Roman should be capable of producing even sharper images than its designers initially expected.

Following the activation of the Wide Field Instrument in September, engineers began a comprehensive testing campaign. They examined the instrument’s 18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note, along with the electronics that operate them. The team then evaluated the element wheel, a rotating mechanism equipped with filters and other optical components, and tested the instrument’s internal calibration system using light-emitting diodes (LEDs) that can produce different colors and brightness levels under commands from Earth. Engineers also tested the instrument’s alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the sharpest images, and checked the thermal control system.

While one group worked on the Wide Field Instrument, another refined the telescope’s overall optical alignment. The results were encouraging from the beginning because Roman’s mirrors and other optical components were already positioned with remarkable accuracy, meaning engineers needed to make only minor corrections. “The telescope’s performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch,” said Matthew Bolcar, Roman’s optical systems lead at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment.”

The team initially concentrated on Roman’s Coronagraph Instrument, which had been producing images that were slightly out of focus. The problem was less severe than engineers had anticipated, making it relatively straightforward to correct. The coronagraph now meets the team’s demanding performance expectations. Engineers will continue refining its camera settings and determining the optimal configurations for its deformable mirrors. In the coming weeks, the team plans to test the coronagraph’s ability to block unwanted light, an essential capability for observing faint objects near much brighter ones. Once the coronagraph’s focus had been optimized, engineers returned to the Wide Field Instrument for another round of adjustments.

stories.headline: SpaceX plans to become a major wireless carrier
body: SpaceX has signaled it is serious about becoming a major wireless carrier in the United States, potentially competing with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon. The company recently agreed to buy a large chunk of low-band spectrum in the 800 MHz range for $8 billion, adding to its previous purchases of EchoStar spectrum worth nearly $20 billion. Combined with FCC approval to deploy 15,000 next-generation Starlink satellites, the moves indicate SpaceX is building toward what it calls "the world's most advanced mobile network."

The 800 MHz spectrum SpaceX just acquired was originally owned by Nextel, the push-to-talk service that Sprint had to divest as part of its merger with T-Mobile. It was sold to private equity firm Grain Management, which held it until SpaceX bought it. According to Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners, the low-band spectrum is critical because it travels farther and provides better coverage, making it essential for a terrestrial network that can support satellite-based mobile service. "Getting this low-band spectrum piece was just an important part, not to make the satellites work better, but to actually give them the spectrum assets that they need to build a terrestrial network," Piecyk said.

SpaceX's strategy has evolved over time. Initially, satellite companies typically do not pay for spectrum, but after positive feedback from investors on its first EchoStar purchase, SpaceX bought more. The company now realizes that to offer mobile service, it needs a terrestrial network to complement its satellites, since satellites alone cannot reliably connect phones inside buildings or with limited power. The existing telecom carriers are unlikely to offer SpaceX a wholesale agreement, forcing SpaceX to build its own infrastructure. Piecyk noted that the stock market reacted to the latest spectrum purchase because investors finally recognized that Elon Musk intends to build a physical network.

The failure of previous attempts to create a fourth wireless carrier in the U.S. — notably by Dish Network and Sprint — raises questions about SpaceX's ability to execute. Dish built some network but could not compete at national scale, and Sprint's attempt to innovate with small cells ultimately failed, leading to its acquisition by T-Mobile. However, Piecyk sees a key difference: "Elon's ability to get customers." He argued that Dish failed not because its network didn't work, but because it could not resonate in the market.

The stakes are high. The U.S. telecom market represents a trillion-dollar enterprise value, and SpaceX has global aspirations for both Starlink and its mobile service. Piecyk suggested that incumbent carriers may have underestimated SpaceX's resolve. "I don't think even these companies were taking Elon seriously and thinking that he would actually build the network," he said. With the spectrum assets now in hand and FCC approval for more satellites, SpaceX appears to be moving from speculation toward a concrete plan to become the fourth major mobile carrier.

stories.headline: Companies Slash AI Budgets After Realizing High Costs and Low-Quality Output
body: A growing number of companies are cutting back on artificial intelligence spending after discovering that their investments are yielding expensive, low-quality results rather than productivity gains. According to reports cited by Futurism, major tech firms including Meta and Microsoft are scaling back ambitious plans to replace staff with AI agents, as executives acknowledge that employees are wasting budgets on costly AI tokens to generate error-ridden content.

Microsoft executive vice president Ryan Roslansky publicly lamented the rise of what he called 'AI slop' in the workplace. 'Someone sent me what was clearly an AI generated doc. I read it, realized it was all AI, had my AI summarize it and ended up with nothing that brought new thinking to the idea… This is a doom loop,' Roslansky wrote on LinkedIn. Johnny Taylor Jr., CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management, told The Guardian that corporate executives feel 'we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,' adding that a more gradual introduction would have been preferable.

The consequences of rushed AI adoption extend beyond wasted money and low-quality output. A September survey by Ernst & Young found that 36 percent of senior AI executives at firms with over $1 billion in annual revenue have already experienced a catastrophic 'AI incident' that caused financial damage, operational disruptions, data loss, or brand damage.

The pullback signals a broader reassessment of AI's practical value in the enterprise. Even companies like Microsoft, whose business model depends on selling AI to others, are rethinking their internal deployment. As the Futurism report notes, the trend reflects a growing realization that the all-out drive to use AI has been a net negative for many organizations, with office workers churning out reams of low-effort AI-generated material rather than achieving meaningful productivity gains.
